## Basis

This report presents the design of a distillation column that separates a key component from a liquid feed by means of fractionation. The design throughput is 41 t per day of feed. The separation duty is the recovery of 88% of the key component at the specified product points: in other words, the column is sized to take that share of the key component overhead while the remainder leaves with the bottoms, and every sizing figure in this report traces back to those two statements. It is important that the duty be stated in this form, as a recovery of a named component, because a design that does not state its duty in that way cannot readily be checked, and stating it here allows the sizing section to be audited against it.

The wetted parts of the column are specified in 316L stainless steel. The grade is fixed here, in the basis, and the materials section will work from it without restating it; corrosion, fabrication and inspection are all assessed against that single specification. No alternative material is carried in the design.

The basis is a steady-state, continuous design. Feed rate, feed condition and product specifications are held at their design values throughout the sizing exercise; departures from those values in actual operation are treated later, in the risks section, rather than by adjusting the basis itself. Physical properties are taken for the design feed composition over the temperature and pressure range that the column internals will see, and the equilibrium data behind the stage calculation belong to the same property set, which ensures that the material balance, the stage count and the hydraulics all rest on one consistent description of the mixture. Utilities are assumed to be available at the battery limit at their normal supply conditions; the reboiler and condenser are sized as part of the column system, and their detailed design follows the same basis. Design margins are not buried in the basis figures: where a margin is applied, it is applied openly in the sizing step that needs it, so that the margin can be located and challenged.

## Sizing

The sizing proceeds in the order in which the calculation depends on itself. The material balance comes first: at 41 t per day of feed and a recovery of 88% of the key component overhead, the distillate and bottoms rates are fixed, and with them the internal liquid and vapour traffic in each section of the column once a reflux condition is chosen. The stage requirement then follows from the equilibrium relation for the mixture and the operating lines that the balance defines; the count obtained in this way is a count of theoretical stages, and it is converted into actual contacting stages through a stage efficiency that reflects the contacting device selected. It should be noted that efficiency is an empirical quantity, and the value adopted belongs to the device and the system, not to the calculation method.

Diameter is set by hydraulics. The column must be able to pass the largest vapour and liquid traffic in each section without flooding, and the diameter is chosen so that the design traffic stands below the flooding limit with the margin that the design practice for the selected internals requires. Diameter and stage count together fix the height: the contacting height from the number of actual stages and their spacing, plus disengaging space above the top stage, feed entry space, and a bottom sump that holds enough liquid for stable level control and pump suction. Pressure drop is calculated stage by stage over the same traffic, because the pressure at the base sets the boiling temperatures that the reboiler must reach and feeds back into the property set. The condenser and reboiler duties come out of the balance around the column at the chosen reflux: the condenser removes the heat that the rising vapour carries in, and the reboiler returns it, and the two duties together close the energy balance on which the sizing stands. A sizing that does not close its own material and energy balances has not been properly checked, and the closure is an integral part of the result.

## Materials

The specification fixed in the basis governs every wetted part: the shell, the internals, the nozzles and the wetted faces of attached equipment are all assessed as one material system. The assessment essentially turns on three key questions. The first question is corrosion: the feed and its products contact the metal over the full temperature range of the column, including the hot base, and the grade is required to resist the mixture as fed, not a cleaned-up version of it; where the feed carries trace components that are known to attack stainless steels, the assessment addresses those components by name rather than the bulk composition. The second question is fabrication: the grade must weld with standard procedures, form to the shell and internals geometry, and accept the surface finish that the contacting devices need in order to seat and seal. The third question is inspection and repair: the material must allow the welds to be examined and local damage to be made good over the life of the unit without resorting to exotic procedures.

Non-wetted parts are separated from this assessment. Supports, external attachments and bolting follow their own specifications and are not upgraded to the wetted grade where the process does not touch them; conversely, no wetted part is value-engineered down to a lesser material, because the corrosion question has already been settled for the grade that the basis fixes. Gaskets and seals are the remaining wetted items that are not metal, and they are selected for compatibility with the same feed over the same temperature range, with the same trace components taken into consideration. A materials section that settles the shell and forgets the gaskets has not, in the end, settled the wetted system as a whole.

## Risks

Two risks are named here as open items, and it should be emphasised that neither of them is resolved in this report.

Fouling is the first. Deposition on the contacting surfaces and in the reboiler degrades a distillation column slowly, and on both of its duties at once: heat transfer falls, so the reboiler delivers less boil-up at the same steam condition, and open area falls, so pressure drop rises and the flooding limit is approached at unchanged throughput. The design as sized carries clean-surface hydraulics, and the fouling tendency of the feed has not been established either by test or by operating history on a comparable service. Until it is, the margin between design traffic and flooding should be read as partly spoken for, and the operating plan should include the pressure-drop trend as the fouling indicator, since pressure drop is the measurement that announces fouling before the separation duty visibly fails.

Turndown is the second risk. The column is sized at its design throughput, and its behaviour well below that rate is not established by the sizing calculation. At low liquid rates, the contacting devices distribute liquid less evenly, and at low vapour rates some devices weep, passing liquid downward without the contact that the stage count assumes; either effect spends separation that the design counted on, so the duty of 88% recovery is not guaranteed at deep turndown by anything in this report. The control range of the reflux and level loops over the same span is likewise untested. Turndown is therefore recorded here as an open item for operating trials, and the report closes with both items still open: fouling untested, turndown untested, and the design valid at the basis on which it was sized.
